summary: Very fast and convenient when new, with a wide mouth that makes scooping and drinking easy. The main complaint is clogging: flow often drops sharply after a few trips or after storage, especially in silty water, and cleaning only sometimes restores it. The soft flasks also develop pinhole leaks. Better suited to short trips with clear water than long thru-hikes.

Very roomy for two and often a palace for one, light for its size, and solid in wind and rain once pitched properly. The main downside is a large footprint that is hard to fit into crowded or uneven sites, plus a learning curve to get a taut pitch. Some report condensation. Too big for a few solo hikers, though many enjoy the extra space.

Praised for generous vestibules, headroom and storm performance, and for being simple to pitch once the technique is learned. The most common drawback is a big footprint that gives a fairly snug sleeping area, which some bigger or taller hikers find cramped, though others of similar height are happy. Suits solo hikers who value weather protection and gear space.

Light and versatile, and many reviewers sleep warm in it, but nearly as many find it colder than its rating. Drafts when rolling over and down shifting or cold spots come up often, and comfort limits are frequently reported well above the rated temperature. Works best with pad straps, a draft collar and layers, and best for people who sleep warm.

Light and comfortable for many, with roomy, well-placed pockets and a good price for the weight. Complaints fall into two groups: comfort problems such as a slipping hip belt, shoulder pain and back sweat, especially with heavier loads, and thin fabric that tears or frays. Best for moderate loads on established trails.

Comfortable for most reviewers, carrying heavy loads well while staying light, roomy and good value. Some find it does not fit them, with hip belt, shoulder or frame issues, and a sweaty back comes up often. Water resistance is a plus for several.

Very durable and comfortable at moderate loads, with an adjustable hip belt, plenty of room and a good fit for a bear canister. Comfort fades once loads climb past roughly 30 to 35 lb, and a few report a sweaty back or poor fit on thin frames. Not the lightest, and can be more pack than a small kit needs. Customer service is praised.

Long-lived and trusted by many, often paired with a CNOC bag for gravity filtering, and easy to backflush. The main complaint is slowing or clogging, especially after storage or in silty water, which some revive with soaking and backflushing and others never fully fix. Squeezing bags by hand gets tedious on long trips.

Fuel efficient, light, quick to boil and strong in wind, with good flame control. The main weak spot is the piezo igniter, which can fail or stop working when wet, so many carry a backup lighter. It is also bulky to nest in small pots with a canister, and some find the pot stand fussy.

Roomy, light, packs small and easy to pitch for many once the technique is learned, with good value. The main complaint is condensation, with damp heads and footboxes where the walls sag, especially for taller sleepers. The pitch has to be exact to avoid sagging, and some find it too short or confining.

Comfortable for most, with a light frame that moves weight to the hips and a surprisingly roomy interior for its size. Fit varies, and some find it uncomfortable at heavier loads or too small in the pockets for bottles. A few report durability problems such as the frame poking through the base or hip belt tearing, several on early versions.

Light and packable, and warm for many reviewers, who take it near or below the rating with layers. A sizable group find it colder than rated, with drafts and down shifting in the long baffles. Ratings read more like limits than comfort figures, so it suits those who sleep warm or choose a warmer version.

Fast flow, easy to backflush with a bottle, a field integrity check and caps on both ends make it a favorite for many, often preferred over a Sawyer. Quality control is the main worry: some units arrive duds, fail the integrity test or have poor flow, and a few clog on silty water and never recover.

Very light, compact and comfortable, and quieter than the XLite. The main complaint is fragility, with punctures, slow leaks and baffle or valve failures, sometimes within weeks. Many use a thin foam pad underneath and carry a repair kit. Also not very warm near freezing for some.

Tough and water resistant, and comfortable for many at moderate loads. The main complaint is shoulder pain with heavier loads, thin straps and no load lifters, with several reaching their limit around 25 to 30 lb. Price and hard-to-reach bottle pockets also come up. Best for lighter kits.

Light, roomy and storm-worthy, with a quick pitch once learned. Downsides are a big footprint that is hard to place on uneven or tight sites, some condensation, and a floor some find delicate. A few find it tight for two or for tall sleepers, who often lie diagonally.

Very comfortable, especially for side sleepers thanks to raised rails, and warm enough for many in cool weather. A good number find it colder than its rating near or below freezing, and some report leaks, loose insulation or weld pinholes. It is on the heavy side and a few find it noisy.

Roomy, freestanding and solid in wind and rain, and quick to pitch for most. It is not the lightest for a solo tent. A few report durability problems with poles, inner mesh or floor, and some find the single-door layout or the shape fiddly or confining.

Comfortable, especially for side sleepers, and warm enough for cold nights, while staying light and packing small. Downsides are scattered: some still feel cold or find it balloon-like, a few find it noisy, and a few report leaks.
Compact, sturdy and good value, with stable pot supports, good wind resistance and a solid simmer. The weak spot is the built-in piezo igniter, which a few say failed. Some find it loud.
